title: Review & Explore Linear Independence
description: Flashcards and interactive examples on linear independence of vectors in 2D and 3D.

steps.speaker: Teacher
steps.message: Hi, let’s review what we learned about linear (in)dependence so far and then explore more.

flashcards.frontText: One vector is a multiple of another

steps.speaker: Assistant
steps.message: Perfect, now let's go back to the parallelism from the last lecture.

steps.speaker: Assistant
steps.message: These two vectors are parallel, so I can right away say that they are linearly dependent.

steps.speaker: Assistant
steps.message: And these two are not parallel, so they are linearly independent.

steps.speaker: Teacher
steps.message: Can I use this simple rule in 3D as well?

answers.feedback: Unfortunately, no, we’ll see soon why.
Correct! The parallel ones are always dependent. But what about independence?
Actually, the parallel ones are always dependent. But what about independence?

steps.speaker: Teacher
steps.message: Well, if we directly see that two vectors are parallel, then one can be expressed as a multiple of the other, so they are definitely dependent.

steps.speaker: Teacher
steps.message: But what about a set of these three vectors: a, b, and c?

answers.feedback: Correct! One vector can be expressed as a combination of the others.
Try thinking how to combine a and c to get b.

steps.speaker: Teacher
steps.message: Look, how 2a + c results in vector b. That shows dependence.

steps.speaker: Assistant
steps.message: And if we have 3 independent vectors, say u=(1, 2, 3), v=(1, 0, 0) and w = (0, 1, 1), how can we confirm the independence?

steps.speaker: Teacher
steps.message: Algebraically confirming independence for any 3D vectors will be our next lesson.
